alternative_readings: If outside the retained HTML body means outside the main circular text, the separate appendix locator and the circular’s cross-references support that document-location inference. If it means absent from the joined packet, it is incorrect: the supplied appendix includes Parts A and B, all three numbered pages and both footnotes.

Legislative references identify definitions and governing regimes; they do not establish formal incorporation of every provision of the named ordinances. The packet contains references and summaries, rather than the complete legislative provisions.

The appendix’s non-exhaustive character does not make the circular’s due-diligence and risk-management expectations optional. Equally, its examples and conditional language do not establish that every illustrated control is universally mandatory. Part A’s technology-audit discussion includes third-party reliance conditions and a footnote addressing blockchain use as a secondary record.

Paragraph 18’s reference to both appendix parts does not expressly expand Part B beyond its stated bearer-form, permissionless-token, public-permissionless-network scope. Part B(f)’s omnibus-account exception concerns segregation from other customers’ assets; it does not extend to segregation from custodian or sub-custodian assets.

Paragraph 26’s position on a mandatory professional-investor-only restriction remains qualified by paragraph 27’s public-offering regimes. Paragraphs 28–29 distinguish the virtual-asset portfolio Terms and Conditions from continuing tokenised-securities obligations. Paragraphs 30–31 describe a case-by-case application for compensation-coverage exclusion, not an automatic exemption.

Paragraph 21 expressly says the circular supersedes the 2019 Statement. It does not establish that this circular remains current at any later assessment date. The remaining guidance on complexity, disclosure, Digital Securities and notification supplies context, but neither reproduces the missing legislation nor proves transaction-specific applicability.

evidence.quote: 14.  In assessing the risks related to the technical and other aspects of Tokenised Securities, an intermediary is suggested to take into account the list of non-exhaustive factors set out in Part A of the Appendix to this circular.

15.  For custodial arrangements, intermediaries should take into account the features and risks of the Tokenised Securities in considering the most appropriate custodial arrangement for the Tokenised Securities to manage ownership and technology risks. Additional considerations for the custodial arrangement for bearer form Tokenised Securities which use permissionless tokens on public-permissionless networks are set out in Part B of the Appendix to this circular.

18.  Intermediaries should understand and be satisfied with the controls implemented by the issuers and their third-party vendors/service providers to manage ownership and technology risks of the Tokenised Securities before they engage in related activities. Please refer to Parts A and B of the Appendix to this circular for a non-exhaustive list of factors for consideration.
Part A: List of non-exhaustive factors for intermediaries’ consideration
Part B: Additional considerations on the custodial arrangement for bearer form
Tokenised Securities using permissionless tokens on public-permissionless networks

5.    There is currently no universal definition or taxonomy for categorising tokenised securities and many different structures may exist in the market. For the purpose of this circular, tokenised securities are traditional financial instruments (eg, bonds or funds) that are “securities” as defined in section 1 of Part 1 of Schedule 1 to the Securities and Futures Ordinance (Cap. 571) (SFO) which utilise DLT (such as blockchain technology) or similar technology in their security lifecycle (Tokenised Securities).

7.    At the outset, given that the nature of Tokenised Securities are fundamentally traditional securities with a tokenisation wrapper, the existing legal and regulatory requirements governing the traditional securities markets continue to apply to Tokenised Securities. In particular, offerings of Tokenised Securities would be subject to the prospectus regime under the Companies (Winding up and Miscellaneous Provisions) Ordinance (Cap. 32) (C(WUMP)O) and the offers of investments regime under Part IV of the SFO. Conduct of intermediaries in the distribution of or advising on Tokenised Securities, management of Tokenised Securities in the form of tokenised funds, management of funds investing in Tokenised Securities and secondary market trading of Tokenised Securities on virtual asset trading platforms are also governed by existing conduct requirements for securities-related activities.

27.  However, intermediaries are reminded that the requirements of the prospectus regime under the C(WUMP)O and the offers of investments regime under Part IV of the SFO would apply to the offering of Tokenised Securities to the public of Hong Kong (Public Offering Regimes). This means that an offer of Tokenised Securities that is not authorised under Part IV of the SFO or which has not complied with the prospectus regime could only be made to PIs or pursuant to any other applicable exemption under the Public Offering Regimes.

28.  In the Joint circular on intermediaries’ virtual asset-related activities, the SFC has clarified that the “de minimis threshold”7  under the Terms and Conditions only applies to virtual assets as defined in section 53ZRA of the AMLO. In other words, the SFC would not impose the Terms and Conditions on fund managers managing portfolios investing in Tokenised Securities meeting the “de minimis threshold” unless the portfolios also invest in virtual assets meeting the “de minimis threshold”.

7 Under the terms and conditions for licensed corporations or registered institutions which manage portfolios that invest in virtual assets (Terms and Conditions), “de minimis threshold” refers to the situation where either: (a) the stated investment objective of a fund is to invest in virtual assets or (b) the intention of a fund is to invest 10% or more of its gross asset value (GAV) in virtual assets. “Virtual asset” is as defined in section 53ZRA of the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance (Cap. 615) (AMLO).

2 For example, a native token with all the characteristics of a collective investment scheme (CIS) (but not simply a tokenised fund) trading on a public-permissionless network. Under the SFO, a CIS generally has four elements: (i) it must involve an arrangement in respect of property; (ii) participants do not have day-to-day control over the management of the property; (iii) the property is managed as a whole by or on behalf of the person operating the arrangement and/or the contributions of the participants and the profits or income from which payments are made to them are pooled; and (iv) the purpose or effect of the arrangement is for participants to participate in or receive profits, income or other returns from the acquisition or management of the property.

missing_premises: Official provenance and completeness of the circular and appendix, their association with the relevant published version, and amendment or supersession history. The supplied locators and hashes establish neither authenticity nor currentness.

The relevant-date official text of SFO (Cap. 571), Schedule 1, Part 1, section 1, including the securities definition and relevant collective-investment-scheme definition, exclusions and cross-references. Footnote 2 supplies only a general CIS summary.

The relevant operative provisions of SFO Part IV and the Cap. 32 prospectus regime, including authorisation requirements, professional-investor definitions and all conditions of any relied-upon exemption. The circular does not enumerate every necessary provision.

The relevant-date official text of AMLO (Cap. 615), section 53ZRA, including exclusions and cross-references. The portfolio threshold described in footnote 7 belongs to the referenced Terms and Conditions; the packet does not establish that it is a statutory threshold.

The governing laws and provisions needed to determine settlement finality, ownership, enforceability, security interests and required regulatory approvals for the actual arrangement. Part A raises these issues without identifying all applicable enactments.
The assessment date and facts about the instrument, intermediary, activity, investors, offering, authorisations, exemptions, network, token form and custody arrangements.

Relevant versions of separately referenced regulatory materials: the authorised-investment-product circular, joint virtual-asset circular, portfolio-management Terms and Conditions, online-distribution guidelines, Code of Conduct, complexity guidance and VATP guidelines. The BIS and GFMA reports are additional conceptual references, not supplied legislative authority.

proposition: The appendix-content gap is resolved within the supplied packet, but the requested official-authority gap is only partly addressed. The main circular expressly refers to Appendix Part A in paragraph 14, Part B in paragraph 15, and both parts in paragraph 18. The separately supplied three-page appendix contains the referenced considerations: Part A covers providers, technology, legal status, continuity, privacy and money-laundering risks; Part B addresses custody for bearer-form Tokenised Securities using permissionless tokens on public-permissionless networks. Its separate location is an inference from the packet’s document structure, not an express legal proposition. The complete legislative texts remain absent: paragraphs 5–7 and 27 refer to SFO definitions and public-offering regimes, while paragraph 28 and footnote 7 refer to AMLO section 53ZRA. Neither the circular’s summaries nor the appendix’s general references to governing laws establish every operative provision or exemption. Accordingly, the appendix is available as retained source text; official provenance, complete legislative authority, currentness and application remain unresolved. This is a source-answer proposal, not legal proof.
